To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the coefficient λ₃, which is a new coefficient in conformal relativistic second-order hydrodynamics, is nonzero and can be calculated directly by Euclidean methods, and (ii) the second-order hydrodynamic transport coefficients τ(Π) and λ₂ are related to the retarded three-point functions of the energy-momentum tensor, which in turn can be calculated from the spectral density.
the second-order hydrodynamical coefficient λ₃ does not in general equal zero, and that its Euclidean correlator is a nontrivial, nonlocal function of the temperature.
(1) the coefficient λ₃ is nonzero in the absence of parity violation and (2) λ₃ and λ₂ are related via a Ward identity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the hydrodynamic behavior of relativistic fluids, in particular with the study of transport coefficients.
the study of hydrodynamic fluctuations in relativistic systems.
the study of hydrodynamical transport coefficients, in particular with their determination by means of Kubo formulas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, while the first-order hydrodynamics is fully determined by the equilibrium two-point correlation functions, the second-order hydrodynamics requires knowledge of the fully retarded three-point function of the stress tensor.
there are 5 independent second-order coefficients, and 3 of these are related by a single Kubo formula to the Euclidean correlation function.
the second-order coefficients λ₃, λ₁ and λ₂ are non-zero in general.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the λ₃ coefficient is the only second-order hydrodynamical coefficient which is nonzero and nonuniversal.
the second-order transport coefficients are all related to three-point functions.
the λ₃ term in the hydrodynamic equations is not a higher-order effect in the gradient expansion, and it is not a consequence of the conformal symmetry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the second-order hydrodynamical equations are not uniquely fixed by the second-order transport equations, but depend also on the three-point functions of the stress-tensor.
, in contrast to the case of the viscosity η, the second-order coefficients cannot be determined from the equilibrium two-point function.
the second-order hydrodynamic equations of motion are not invariant under the full group of conformal transformations, but only under the smaller group of "conformal Galilean" transformations.
